5080: When you call something or someone elfin, you are saying it has the qualities of an elf — but not the scary or monstrous kind. Think of the classic image of an elf from folklore and fairy tales: a small, slender, magical creature with delicate features, light movements, and a slightly mischievous sparkle. Elfin captures all of that in a single word.

Elfin bundles together several qualities at once. Something elfin is:

  • Small and delicate — not in a weak or frail way, but in a fine-boned, graceful way. Think of features that are neat, precise, and almost too perfect.
  • Charming and otherworldly — there is something magical or fairy-like about it, as if it doesn't quite belong to the ordinary world.
  • Slightly mischievous — a hint of playful, impish energy. Not naughty, but not completely innocent either. There's a quiet twinkle to it.
  • Light and nimble — elfin things seem effortless, unburdened, quick.

The key is that elfin is not just about being small. A mouse is small. A pebble is small. Neither is elfin. Something elfin has that additional layer of magic, charm, and delicate beauty. Size is only part of the picture.
Who or What Can Be Called Elfin?

Elfin is most commonly used to describe a person's physical appearance or manner, though it can apply to other things too.

A person's face or features — this is the most common use. An elfin face typically has large, expressive eyes, a small nose, sharp or fine cheekbones, and an overall look that feels delicate and a little magical. Think of someone who looks like they could slip into a forest and disappear.

"She had an elfin face — wide eyes, a pointed chin, and the kind of look that made you feel she knew a secret."

A person's build or figure — elfin describes someone who is slender and slight, but with a graceful quality. They don't seem heavy or clunky. They move lightly.

"He was a small, elfin figure who moved through the crowd without making a sound."

A person's smile or expression — an elfin smile is one with a hint of mischief and delight in it, a little knowing, as if the person is amused by something they won't tell you.

"She gave an elfin smile and refused to answer."

A person's manner or personality — someone elfin might be playful, quick-witted, light-hearted, and hard to pin down. There's an airy, mysterious quality to them.

"There was something elfin about him — he seemed to appear and disappear at will, always laughing."

A place or scene (less common, but valid) — a forest clearing bathed in soft light, a hidden garden, a quiet moonlit glade — these can feel elfin when they carry that sense of magic and enchantment.

This is important, because the word sounds like it might mean something eerie or strange. It does not.

  • Elfin does not mean ugly or weird. It is almost always a compliment, or at the very least, neutral-to-positive.
  • Elfin does not mean childlike in a patronising way. It doesn't mean immature. It means someone has a certain ageless, magical quality — like they exist slightly outside of time.
  • Elfin does not mean "tiny" in a negative sense. Being described as elfin is not the same as being called short in an unflattering way. The word romanticises and elevates smallness.
  • Elfin does not mean clumsy or eccentric. The elf it evokes is elegant, not awkward.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Elfin is a warm, slightly poetic word. When a writer uses it, they are doing more than describing size — they are painting a picture of something enchanting, light, and slightly beyond the ordinary. It carries a sense of wonder and admiration.

It sits comfortably in literary writing, descriptions of people in novels, and everyday compliments. It is not slang, not rude, not technical. It is the kind of word a writer reaches for when they want to describe someone who seems too graceful and fine-featured to be entirely of this world.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Pixie-like — very similar to elfin. A pixie is also a small, mischievous magical creature. If elfin slightly emphasises delicate beauty and an otherworldly quality, pixie-like emphasises the playful, cheeky side a little more.

Delicate — overlaps with elfin in describing fine features, but has no magical quality. A china cup is delicate. A person with an elfin face is more than just delicate.

Petite — describes small physical size in women, but is plain and descriptive, with no enchantment or mischievousness attached.

Impish — captures the mischievous side of elfin, but not the delicate beauty or magical quality.

So elfin is the only word that combines all four qualities — small, delicate, charming, and slightly magical — in one.

Elfin means having the qualities of an elf — small, fine-featured, delicately beautiful, with a light, charming, slightly mischievous, and otherworldly quality about it. It is a compliment that says: there is something magical here.
5081:
To elicit something means to draw out or bring out a response, reaction, feeling, or piece of information from a person — something that was already inside them, waiting to come out.

Think of it this way: imagine a teacher in a classroom who doesn't just lecture. Instead, she asks clever questions that pull out the right answers from the students themselves. She is eliciting those answers. She didn't put the knowledge there — it was already in the students — but her skill and technique brought it to the surface.

That's the heart of the word. Something was latent (existing but not yet expressed), and someone — or something — caused it to emerge.
The Key Idea That Makes It Precise

The word carries two quiet but important ideas bundled inside it:

1. The thing being drawn out already existed.
You don't elicit something you create from scratch. You elicit something that was already there — a feeling, a fact, an opinion, a reaction — but hadn't come out yet.

2. There is usually some skill, effort, or deliberate action involved.
Eliciting isn't accidental. A bad joke might accidentally get a laugh. But a comedian who crafts a perfect punchline and reliably draws laughter — they are eliciting it. The word has a slightly intentional, purposeful flavour.

Almost any kind of response or reaction:

Emotions and physical reactions — A moving speech can elicit tears. A funny remark can elicit laughter. A shocking photo can elicit gasps.

Information — A detective's careful questioning can elicit a confession. A doctor's gentle manner can elicit honest answers from a nervous patient.

Opinions and thoughts — A survey is designed to elicit people's views. A great interviewer elicits stories you've never heard the guest tell before.

Biological or scientific reactions — Scientists use the word too. A drug can elicit a reaction in the body. A stimulus can elicit a response in the brain.
Who or What Can Elicit Something?

A person can elicit a response from another person — but so can a thing. Both of these sentences are correct:

  • "Her calm tone elicited a more open and honest reply from him."
  • "The film's ending elicited strong emotions from the audience."

In the first, a person's behaviour does the eliciting. In the second, a piece of art does it. The word works in both situations.
How It Differs From Similar Words

This is where you really nail the word down. Several words feel similar but aren't quite the same.

Elicit vs. Provoke — To provoke often suggests a stronger, more negative push, and sometimes implies that you're intentionally causing anger or conflict. Eliciting is more neutral and often positive. A teacher elicits answers; a bully provokes a fight.

Elicit vs. Evoke — Evoke leans heavily toward feelings and memories, and suggests they arise somewhat automatically and powerfully, often in an artistic or emotional context. A piece of music evokes nostalgia. A skilled questioner elicits information. Evoking happens more passively inside you; eliciting is more about what someone does to bring something out of you.

Elicit vs. Extract — Extract suggests more force, almost as though you're pulling something out against resistance — like extracting a tooth, or extracting a secret from someone who doesn't want to share. Eliciting is gentler and more skilful. A torturer extracts a confession; a skilled therapist elicits one.

Elicit vs. Prompt — Prompt means to trigger or cause someone to act or speak, but it's more mechanical and doesn't carry the sense that something was already "inside" the person. Prompting is a nudge; eliciting is a draw.
Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

Elicit is a formal word. You'll find it most often in writing and speech that is professional, academic, or analytical — journalism, psychology, medicine, academic papers, legal contexts, and formal interviews. In everyday casual conversation, people are more likely to say "get," "draw out," or "bring out" instead. But elicit is never wrong to use; it's simply elevated.

To sound natural using this word, notice the phrases it commonly appears in:

  • elicit a response
  • elicit a reaction
  • elicit information
  • elicit laughter / tears / sympathy / outrage / surprise
  • elicit feedback
  • elicit a confession
  • elicit answers (from students)
  • elicit a smile
A Critical Warning: Don't Confuse It With "Illicit"

This is one of the most common mix-ups in English.

  • Elicit (verb) = to draw out a response ("The question elicited a strong answer.")
  • Illicit (adjective) = illegal, forbidden, or morally wrong ("an illicit deal")

They sound almost identical when spoken, but they mean completely different things and belong to different word classes. Illicit is an adjective describing something forbidden. Elicit is a verb describing an action. When in doubt, remember: if you can replace the word with "illegal," you want illicit. If you can replace it with "draw out," you want elicit.
A Final Sentence to Lock It In

If you remember only one sentence, let it be this:

To elicit is to skillfully draw out something — a feeling, a fact, or a reaction — that was already inside a person, through deliberate words or actions.
5082: To elide something means to leave it out — to cause it to disappear, either by cutting it, skipping over it, or merging it into something else so smoothly that it vanishes without a trace. The word is used in three main situations, and understanding all three gives you full ownership of it.
1. In Speech: Dropping a Sound or Syllable

This is the most concrete use. When people speak naturally and quickly, they often drop certain sounds without realizing it. That dropping is eliding.

When you say "ev'ry" instead of "every," you are eliding the middle syllable. When "I am" becomes "I'm," the vowel is elided. When "going to" softens into "gonna" in casual speech, the sounds in between are being elided. The key thing to notice is that the sound disappears so naturally that speech still flows without interruption. There's no awkward gap where the missing sound was.
2. In Writing: Cutting a Portion of a Text

When an editor, journalist, or author removes a section of a speech, document, or quotation — especially to shorten it — they elide that portion.

Imagine a journalist quoting a ten-paragraph speech in an article. She includes only three paragraphs and skips the rest. She has elided the other seven. The ellipsis you often see in quotations (…) is the visual signal that something has been elided — that a chunk of text was removed and the remaining parts were joined together.
3. In Arguments and Thinking: Glossing Over a Distinction

This is the most powerful and most commonly encountered use of the word, especially in academic and critical writing. When someone — in an essay, a debate, or an argument — quietly ignores an important difference between two things, or treats two separate ideas as if they're the same without justifying why, we say they have elided that distinction.

This usage almost always carries a critical edge. Saying someone "elides" something implies: you skipped over something important that you should have addressed.

Consider these examples. "The author elides the crucial difference between being poor and being lazy." This means the author quietly treats two very different things as equivalent, hoping you won't notice. "The politician's speech elides the fact that crime was already falling before his policy took effect." He glossed over an inconvenient truth. "The essay elides important distinctions between the two historical events." The two events are being treated as the same when they clearly aren't.

In this sense, to elide is to sweep something under the rug — to remove it so smoothly that a gap in the logic goes unnoticed.

Every use of elide shares a single core idea: something is removed or merged so it disappears from view. Whether it's a sound in speech, a paragraph in a text, or a crucial distinction in an argument — the result is the same. It's no longer visible. The seam where it was is closed up.

This is an important nuance. "Omit" simply means to leave something out — it's neutral and blunt. "Elide" means to leave something out in a way that is smooth or seamless, where the removal allows everything around it to flow together as though the missing piece was never there. There's an elegance — sometimes a suspicious elegance — to eliding.

Furthermore, "elide" in the analytical sense often implies the omission is problematic. You're not just noting that something was left out; you're pointing out that something was conveniently avoided.

The noun form is elision — the act or instance of eliding something. "The elision of that syllable is natural in spoken French." "The elision of this counterargument seriously weakens the essay's case." You'll encounter this form often in linguistics and literary criticism.

Here are clean examples across all its uses so the word feels familiar in context:

"The film elides decades of history in a single two-minute montage."
"Speakers naturally elide certain consonants when talking fast."
"The report elides several inconvenient facts about the policy's failures."
"Be careful not to elide the distinction between correlation and causation."
"The biography elides the most controversial years of his life entirely."

Think of elide as the verb for a smooth, seamless omission — something is dropped or merged so neatly that the join barely shows. That smoothness, and the sometimes deliberate nature of it, is what separates it from blunter words like cut, skip, or drop. When you see or use elide, something has been made to disappear — and the disappearance was intentional enough to deserve a name.
5083:
Eligible means: you qualify to receive, do, or be considered for something because you meet the required conditions.

The key idea is always about conditions. Someone — an organization, a government, a school, a competition — sets certain rules or criteria. If you satisfy those criteria, you are eligible. If you don't, you are ineligible (the opposite).

Being eligible doesn't mean you will get something. It means you can be considered for it. You have cleared the first gate.
A Simple Example to Lock It In

Imagine a company offering a scholarship. They say: "Only students above 18 years of age, studying science, with grades above 80% may apply."

  • A 20-year-old science student with 85% grades → eligible
  • A 16-year-old science student with 90% grades → not eligible (too young)
  • A 22-year-old arts student with 85% grades → not eligible (wrong subject)

The student who meets all the stated conditions is eligible. The others are not — even if they are otherwise talented or deserving. Eligibility is always measured against specific, defined criteria, not general worthiness.

1. eligible for + (noun)
This is used when the result is a thing — a benefit, an award, a position, a scheme.

"She is eligible for the promotion."
"He is eligible for a tax refund."
"Citizens over 60 are eligible for the pension."

2. eligible to + (verb)
This is used when the result is an action — something you are allowed to do.

"You must be 18 to be eligible to vote."
"Only registered members are eligible to participate."
"She became eligible to apply after completing her degree."

Both patterns are extremely common. Knowing both will cover almost every real-world usage you encounter.
Shades of Meaning Across Different Situations

In government and law:
Eligibility is usually tied to age, citizenship, income, or residence. There is no negotiation — you either satisfy the criteria or you don't.

"Only citizens are eligible for this government scheme."

In jobs and careers:
Eligibility is typically tied to qualifications, experience, or seniority.

"Candidates with less than two years of experience are not eligible for this role."

In competitions and sports:
Rules define who may participate or be selected.

"Players who have already won the award are not eligible to be nominated again."

In finance:
Banks, insurance companies, and lenders use eligibility to decide who qualifies for a loan, a card, or a plan.

"Your credit score makes you eligible for a lower interest rate."

In social usage — "eligible bachelor/bachelorette":
This is a fixed, culturally established phrase. An eligible bachelor is a man who is unmarried, financially stable, and considered a desirable candidate for marriage. It has nothing to do with formal criteria — it just means society views him as a "good catch."

"He's young, successful, and single — quite an eligible bachelor."

Eligible ≠ Capable
Capable means you have the skill or ability to do something. Eligible means you meet the formal requirements to be considered. A brilliant 15-year-old might be capable of doing a university course, but not eligible to enroll (due to age requirements).

Eligible ≠ Selected or Chosen
Being eligible is just the starting point. Out of 500 eligible candidates, only 10 might be selected. Eligibility opens the door; it doesn't guarantee you walk through it.

Eligible ≠ Entitled
Entitled means you have a right to something. Eligible is softer — it means you qualify to be considered, but the final decision may still rest with someone else.

These are the most natural ways "eligible" is used in real language:

  • become eligible — "You become eligible once you turn 21."
  • remain eligible — "Stay enrolled to remain eligible for the grant."
  • no longer eligible — "After missing the deadline, she was no longer eligible."
  • make someone eligible — "This certificate makes you eligible to teach."
  • eligible voters — all people who meet the criteria to vote in an election
  • eligible candidates — those who qualify to run for a position or apply for something
  • deemed eligible — formally judged to meet the criteria (used in official/legal contexts)

QuestionAnswer
What does it mean?You meet the required conditions to receive, do, or be considered for something
Does it guarantee the outcome?No — it only means you qualify to be considered
What are the two main patterns?eligible for (thing) and eligible to (action)
What is the opposite?Ineligible

In short: whenever you see "eligible," ask yourself — "what are the conditions, and does this person meet them?" That question will always unlock the exact meaning, no matter the context.
5084:
To eliminate something means to completely remove it, get rid of it, or put an end to it — so thoroughly that it no longer exists or no longer plays any role in a situation.

The key idea is totality. You are not reducing something, not pushing it aside temporarily, not hiding it — you are making it disappear entirely from the picture.

Think of a whiteboard with writing on it. When you erase a single word, you've removed it. When you eliminate all the writing, the board is completely blank — nothing remains. That sense of complete, final removal is what "eliminate" is all about.

"Eliminate" is used in several distinct situations. All of them share that core idea of complete removal, but they apply it differently.

1. To completely remove a problem, risk, or unwanted thing

This is the most common and general use. When you eliminate something, you take action to make sure it is fully gone — not just reduced, but entirely dealt with.

  • "The new vaccine helped eliminate the disease from the country."
  • "We must eliminate all errors before submitting the report."
  • "Her goal is to eliminate poverty in the region."
  • "Regular exercise can help eliminate certain health risks."

Notice: in each case, the aim is zero — zero errors, zero disease, zero poverty. Not less of it. None of it.

2. To rule something out — to conclude that it is not possible, not relevant, or not responsible

When you are investigating, reasoning, or choosing between options, you can "eliminate" a possibility once you've determined it doesn't apply. You are removing it from your consideration entirely.

  • "The detective eliminated two suspects after checking their alibis."
  • "We can eliminate option C — it doesn't meet our requirements."
  • "After running the tests, doctors eliminated cancer as a possible cause."
  • "By the process of elimination, she figured out the correct answer."

This meaning is especially common in detective work, scientific reasoning, decision-making, and diagnosis. You eliminate what you know is wrong, so you can focus on what might be right.

3. To defeat someone and remove them from a competition

In sports, tournaments, and contests, when a team or player is eliminated, they have lost and can no longer continue. They are out — there is no coming back into the competition.

  • "Argentina was eliminated in the semifinals."
  • "Three teams were eliminated in the first round of the tournament."
  • "She was eliminated from the singing competition after her performance on Friday."

This meaning comes directly from the general idea: the person or team is "removed" from the competition entirely.

4. To kill someone (formal, euphemistic)

In military, espionage, and very formal or cold language, "eliminate" is sometimes used to mean to kill, especially when referring to a target, an enemy, or a threat. It is a deliberate euphemism — a softer-sounding word chosen specifically to create emotional distance from the act.

  • "The soldiers were ordered to eliminate the target."
  • "The spy's mission was to eliminate the enemy commander."

You will encounter this in news articles, novels, and films involving military or intelligence contexts. It does not mean this in everyday use — if someone says "I want to eliminate this problem," they are not talking about killing anything. Context makes it clear.

5. To remove a variable from a mathematical equation

In algebra and higher mathematics, when you "eliminate" a variable, you manipulate two or more equations to remove one variable so you can solve for the others.

  • "Eliminate x from the system of equations to find the value of y."

You may encounter this in school or academic settings.

Once you understand the core, you'll notice a few things that are always true of "eliminate":

It implies completeness. You eliminate something entirely. This is what separates it from words like "reduce" or "decrease." If a company reduces waste, some waste still remains. If it eliminates waste, none remains.

It implies intentionality. Eliminate is almost always used for a deliberate act. Someone decides to eliminate something and takes action. You wouldn't say a disease accidentally eliminated itself.

It often implies finality. When something is eliminated, the goal is for it to stay gone. It is not a temporary removal — it is meant to be permanent.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding "eliminate" fully means understanding how it differs from related words:

Get rid of — means the same thing in casual speech, but is very informal. "Get rid of the bugs" and "eliminate the bugs" mean the same thing; the first is casual, the second is more formal.

Remove — broader and more neutral. You can remove something temporarily or partially. Remove does not carry the "completely, finally, no more" weight that eliminate does.

Eradicate — nearly identical in strength to "eliminate," but used almost exclusively for deeply rooted, widespread problems: diseases, poverty, a species of pest. "Eradicate smallpox" sounds natural; "eradicate a typo" does not.

Abolish — used specifically for laws, rules, systems, practices, and institutions. You abolish slavery, abolish a law, abolish a tradition. You don't "abolish" a disease or a math variable.

Exterminate — means to completely destroy a large number of living things (insects, rodents, and, in its darkest uses, people). It carries a more brutal and destructive tone.

Exclude — means to keep something out or leave something out, but not necessarily because it has been defeated or destroyed. You exclude a possibility when it doesn't apply; you eliminate it when you've proven it doesn't apply.

"Eliminate" is almost always followed by a noun — the thing being eliminated. Here are common patterns:

  • eliminate + a problem/threat/risk/danger — the most common pattern
  • eliminate + waste/poverty/hunger/violence — abstract social or systemic issues
  • eliminate + a suspect/possibility/option — in reasoning or investigation
  • eliminate + someone from a competition — in sports/contests
  • eliminate + a variable — in mathematics

Common adverbs used with it: completely eliminate, totally eliminate, effectively eliminate, help eliminate, seek to eliminate, aim to eliminate.
The Register: When Is This Word Used?

"Eliminate" is a formal to semi-formal word. It appears in:

  • Academic and scientific writing ("The study aims to eliminate bias.")
  • Business and professional language ("We need to eliminate inefficiencies in the process.")
  • News and journalism ("The team was eliminated in the quarterfinals.")
  • Medical and policy language ("Efforts to eliminate tuberculosis globally.")

In everyday spoken conversation, people more often say "get rid of" instead. But "eliminate" is not so formal that it sounds out of place in normal sentences — it sits comfortably in both written and spoken English across most contexts.
One Thing to Be Careful About

Do not confuse eliminate with illuminate. They sound somewhat similar but mean completely different things.

  • Eliminate = to remove completely
  • Illuminate = to light something up, or to make something clearer and easier to understand

This is a common mix-up, so keep an eye on it.

To eliminate means to completely and intentionally remove something — a problem, a possibility, a competitor, a threat — so that it no longer exists or no longer needs to be considered. It always involves totality (not just reduction), intentionality (a deliberate act), and often finality (gone for good). It is versatile across everyday, professional, scientific, and competitive contexts, and sits at a slightly formal register — more precise and weighty than "remove," and stronger than "reduce."
5085:
Elision is the act of leaving something out — specifically, cutting away a sound, syllable, or sometimes an entire passage — to make speech, writing, or thought flow more smoothly or efficiently. The thing that gets cut is the elision. Think of it as deliberate, purposeful omission.

The key word to hold onto is omission. When you elide something, you remove it. You don't replace it with anything. You just leave a gap, and the surrounding material flows together to fill it.
Where you already know it — everyday speech

You perform elision constantly, without realising it. Your mouth naturally seeks the path of least effort. So sounds and syllables quietly vanish to make words easier to say, especially when speaking quickly or casually.

Here are examples you use every day:

  • "I am" → "I'm" — the vowel a disappears. That disappearance is an elision.
  • "do not" → "don't" — the o is dropped.
  • "going to" → "gonna" — multiple sounds are lost.
  • "February" → "Feb-you-ary" in casual speech — the first r sound quietly vanishes.
  • "vegetable" → "veg-ta-ble" — the middle syllable gets swallowed.
  • "camera" → "cam-ra" — the second vowel disappears in fast speech.

In every single one of these, a sound or syllable was cut out. The word got shorter. It got easier to say. That cutting is elision.
The apostrophe — elision's footprint in writing

Whenever elision is recorded in writing, it usually leaves behind an apostrophe (') — a small mark that signals: "something used to live here, and we removed it."

  • I'm — the a from I am was elided; the apostrophe marks the empty space.
  • they're — the a from they are is gone.
  • o'clock — a shortening of of the clock; the f the was elided.
  • rock 'n' roll — both the a and the d of and were elided, leaving just n.

You can think of the apostrophe as a scar left behind by elision — proof that something was once there and got cut away.
Elision in poetry — a deliberate craft tool

While everyday elision happens naturally and without thinking, poets use it on purpose and with great care.

Poetry often follows a strict rhythm — a fixed number of beats or syllables per line. If a word has too many syllables, it can throw the rhythm off, like an extra beat in music. So poets elide syllables deliberately to make words fit the metre without breaking the flow.

In older English poetry especially, you'll see things like:

  • o'er instead of over — one syllable instead of two
  • e'en instead of even
  • ne'er instead of never
  • 'tis instead of it is
  • heav'n instead of heaven

Here, elision isn't laziness — it's a precise technical choice. The poet is sculpting sound. A syllable must go for the line to sing correctly.
A crucial distinction — elision vs. ellipsis

These two words are often confused, and it's worth separating them clearly once.

  • Elision = the cutting of a sound or syllable within a word or between words in speech.
  • Ellipsis = the cutting of whole words or phrases from a sentence when the meaning is still understood from context.

For example: "She can play guitar, and he can too." — The words "play guitar" are left out after "can" because they're already implied. That's ellipsis, not elision. Elision operates at the level of sounds; ellipsis operates at the level of words and grammar. They're neighbours, not twins.
The broader, figurative use — omitting facts or ideas

In more formal writing — journalism, literary criticism, philosophy, legal analysis — elision is also used to describe the deliberate or careless omission of information, facts, or an important part of an argument, not just sounds.

For example:

  • "The report's elision of the contradictory data made its conclusions misleading."
  • "Critics noted the film's troubling elision of the most painful chapter of that history."
  • "His argument worked only because of a quiet elision of the most important counterpoint."

In this usage, elision carries a slightly sharp or critical edge. It implies that something significant was missing — whether through oversight, dishonesty, or stylistic choice. The idea is the same: something that should be there was removed.
The one-sentence definition to remember forever

Elision is the deliberate or natural omission of a sound, syllable, or piece of information — most commonly heard in speech (where sounds vanish for ease of saying), seen in writing (where an apostrophe marks what was removed), practised in poetry (where syllables are cut to maintain rhythm), and used figuratively (where facts or ideas are quietly left out of an argument or account).

If you want one image to lock this word in your memory: think of elision as editing with a pair of scissors — something is snipped out, the remaining pieces are pushed together, and the result is smoother, shorter, and cleaner. What got snipped is the elision.
5086:
When you call something or someone elite, you mean they are among the absolute best — not just good, not just great, but at the very top of their group. It describes people, things, or groups that have reached a level of excellence, skill, power, or quality that very few others can match.

Think of it as a kind of invisible filter. Imagine you take every soldier in the world and keep removing the ones who are slightly less skilled — you keep only the finest, the most capable, the most accomplished. The tiny group left standing at the end? Those are the elite soldiers.

The word carries two ideas together, always:

1. Exceptional quality or ability
Whatever is called elite is not just above average — it is at the very peak. An elite athlete doesn't just train hard; they perform at a level that puts them in the top fraction of a percent of all athletes on earth.

2. Exclusivity
Elite things and people are rare by definition. If everyone could reach that level, the word wouldn't apply anymore. There is always a sense of "very few make it here." Elite implies a narrow, high standard that most people or things simply don't meet.

These two ideas — exceptional quality + rarity — are the soul of the word. Whenever you see "elite," both ideas are present.
How It's Used in Different Areas of Life

The word "elite" travels across many areas of life. Here's how it works in each:

In the military:
An elite unit or elite forces refers to soldiers who are specially selected, exceptionally trained, and highly capable — far beyond regular troops. Think of special forces or navy SEALs. They are called elite because most soldiers cannot meet the extreme standards required to join them.

In sports:
An elite athlete is one who competes at the highest professional or world-class level. They are not just talented — they are among the best performers in their sport globally. A club-level tennis player is good. A national-level player is very good. A player competing for world titles is elite.

In education:
An elite university or elite school is one that has extremely high academic standards, admits very few students, and has a strong reputation for producing outstanding graduates. The selectivity and prestige are both part of what makes it "elite."

In society and social class:
The elite (as a group) refers to people who hold the most power, wealth, or social influence in a society — politicians, billionaires, top executives. When used as an adjective in this sense, something "elite" serves or belongs to this powerful group, such as an "elite social club."

In products and services:
An elite product, service, or membership refers to something of premium, top-tier quality — often expensive, exclusive, and designed to be better than everything else in its category.

It's important to understand that "elite" is a strong word. It is not just a fancy way of saying "good" or "excellent." There is a clear ladder here:

Decent → Good → Excellent → Outstanding → Elite

By the time you reach "elite," you are talking about a level that most people and things never reach. Using the word for something ordinary weakens it and sounds exaggerated. "Elite" should feel earned.
The Tone: Positive, But Sometimes Complicated

Most of the time, "elite" is used positively and admiringly. Calling a team, a skill, or a product "elite" is a genuine compliment — it signals the highest standard.

However, the word can sometimes carry a slightly complicated tone, depending on context:

When it sounds negative or unfair:
If people use "elite" to describe a group that has privilege and power, and that group uses that status to look down on others or keep others out, the word can sound critical. For example, "The elite schools only accept students from wealthy families" suggests something unfair and exclusive — not a compliment, but a criticism.

This negative feeling is often called elitism — the attitude that people or groups who are elite are somehow better as human beings, and that others deserve less. "Elitism" is almost always seen as a bad thing, even though being elite at a skill is generally admired. The difference is:

  • Being an elite surgeon (because of your exceptional skill) = admired
  • Being elitist (thinking you're a superior human being because of your status) = criticized

So the adjective "elite" is positive when it describes genuine excellence. It becomes complicated or critical when it's tied to unfairness, exclusion, or arrogance.

These are natural pairings with "elite" that you'll see and hear often:

  • Elite forces / elite troops — the most highly trained soldiers
  • Elite athlete / elite performer — someone at the peak of their sport or craft
  • Elite institution / elite university — a top-tier, highly selective school
  • Elite level — the highest standard of performance in any field
  • Elite club / elite circle — an exclusive group of highly powerful or accomplished people
  • Elite status — a special recognition given to top customers, members, or performers (commonly used in airlines, loyalty programs, etc.)
A Simple Test for Whether "Elite" Applies

Ask yourself three questions:

  1. Is this among the very best of its kind? (Not just good — the top.)
  2. Is it rare or hard to reach this level? (Can most people or things get here easily? If yes, it's probably not elite.)
  3. Would experts or people in the field agree it's at the top? (Is the standard real, or just self-proclaimed?)

If the answer to all three is yes, "elite" fits perfectly.

Elite describes something or someone that belongs to the very highest level of quality, skill, or status — exceptional enough to stand apart from almost everything else, and rare enough that not everyone can reach it.
5087:
The elite refers to a small, select group of people who are considered the best, most powerful, or most privileged within a larger group or society. The word always carries the idea of standing clearly above the rest — of being at the very top of some kind of ranking or hierarchy.

Think of it this way: if you have a country of millions of people, and only a tiny fraction of them hold the most wealth, power, or influence, that group is the elite.

For a group to be called "the elite," two things must almost always be true:

1. They are a minority. The elite is never the majority. It's a small, concentrated group. If everyone qualifies, the word loses its meaning entirely. The elite exists because most people don't belong to it.

2. They occupy the top. They are superior in some measurable way — whether that's wealth, power, skill, status, or influence. They're not just good. They're the best or most dominant in their domain.

"Elite" as a noun appears in a few forms:

"The elite" is the most common form. It refers to a group and is often treated as a plural noun, even though it looks singular.

"The elite control most of the nation's wealth."
"The elite have always resisted change."

"An elite" refers to one specific group that qualifies as elite within a particular field.

"The special forces are an elite within the military."

"Elites" refers to multiple such groups, often from different domains.

"Political elites and corporate elites often share the same interests."

The word isn't tied to just one area of life. It travels across many domains, and understanding these will sharpen your feel for it:

Social & Economic Elite — This is probably the most common use. It refers to the wealthiest, most privileged class in a society. These are people who were often born into money and status, or who accumulated so much wealth that they now exist in a completely different world from ordinary people.

"The social elite rarely interact with the working class."

Political Elite — Those who hold or influence government power — politicians, policymakers, advisors, and the networks around them.

"The political elite made decisions that affected millions, yet consulted almost no one."

Intellectual Elite — The brightest, most educated, most respected thinkers, academics, or experts in a field.

"The intellectual elite shaped the cultural conversation of the era."

Military Elite — The most highly trained, capable soldiers or units within an armed force.

"Only the most disciplined soldiers are admitted into the military elite."

Athletic or Sporting Elite — The very top performers in a sport, those competing at the highest levels.

"She trained for years before reaching the athletic elite."

The domain changes, but the core idea stays the same: a small group at the very top.
The Tone of the Word — Positive, Negative, or Neutral?

This is where the word gets interesting. "Elite" is not emotionally neutral — it carries different feelings depending on context and the speaker's point of view.

When used admiringly, it suggests excellence, discipline, and achievement. Calling soldiers or athletes "the elite" often carries respect — it means they've reached a level most people cannot.

When used critically, it suggests unfairness, arrogance, exclusivity, or being out of touch with ordinary people. Phrases like "the out-of-touch elite" or "the ruling elite" carry a sharp, resentful edge — the implication being that this group has too much power or privilege, and uses it selfishly.

When used neutrally, it's simply descriptive — the best in a given field, with no judgment attached.

So the same word can be a compliment, a criticism, or a plain fact — depending entirely on the sentence around it and the speaker's intent. Pay close attention to context.
The Hidden Idea Inside the Word

Here is something deeper worth understanding: the word "elite" only makes sense because of contrast. There can be no elite without a much larger group of ordinary or less powerful people below them. The elite are defined by the gap between themselves and everyone else.

This is why the word often appears in discussions about inequality, power, and fairness — because whenever there is an elite, there is, by definition, a majority who are not the elite. That tension is baked right into the word itself.

To sharpen the definition further, here's what the word does not mean:

  • It does not mean simply "good" or "skilled." A decent footballer is not part of the sporting elite. The word demands the highest tier.
  • It does not mean a large group. A group of thousands or millions cannot be "the elite" unless they are a small fraction of an even larger population.
  • It does not always mean deserving. Someone can be part of the elite purely through birth, inheritance, or corrupt power — not merit.

The elite = a small, exclusive group that sits at the top — of a society, an institution, a profession, or any human domain — by virtue of wealth, power, skill, status, or some combination of these. The word can be said with admiration, with resentment, or with plain description. But it always points to the same truth: these people are at the top, and most people are not.
5088:
Elitism is the belief or attitude that a small, select group of people — called "the elite" — are inherently superior to ordinary people, and therefore deserve more power, privilege, status, or influence over society.

The word comes from the idea of an "elite": a tiny group at the top, considered the best, the brightest, or the most powerful. Elitism is not just noticing that such a group exists. It is actively believing that this group deserves to be treated differently — that their opinions matter more, their choices should govern everyone, and that ordinary people are somehow less worthy.

Depending on the context, the "elite" might be defined by:

  • Wealth — the very rich
  • Education — graduates of the most prestigious universities
  • Social class — old aristocratic families, "high society"
  • Intellect — people considered exceptionally intelligent
  • Political power — rulers, top officials, influential networks
  • Cultural taste — people who appreciate "high" art, literature, or music

Elitism is the attitude that any one of these things makes a person fundamentally better than everyone else — and that society should be organized around serving, listening to, or being run by that group.
What Elitism Looks Like in Practice

It helps to see elitism across different areas of life:

Social elitism is the belief that people from wealthy or aristocratic backgrounds are simply better — more refined, more deserving of respect — than those from ordinary or working-class families. A person displaying social elitism might refuse to associate with someone because of their background, even if that person is kind, intelligent, and hardworking.

Intellectual elitism is the belief that highly educated or academically credentialed people should be the ones making decisions, and that the average person's opinion is too uninformed to be worth taking seriously. An intellectually elitist person might dismiss a farmer's or factory worker's political views as naive and not worth hearing, simply because that person doesn't hold a university degree.

Cultural elitism is the belief that certain forms of art, music, and literature — typically classical music, literary fiction, or fine art — are superior, and that people who enjoy popular culture, mainstream entertainment, or "lowbrow" media are less sophisticated or less intelligent. A cultural elitist might openly sneer at someone for enjoying a blockbuster film or a pop song, treating their tastes as a sign of a lesser mind.

Political elitism is the belief that a small class of experts, leaders, or powerful people should govern society, and that ordinary citizens are not capable of understanding or participating meaningfully in how the country is run.

Economic elitism is the belief that the wealthy have earned — and deserve to maintain — their dominant position in society, and that policies should be shaped to serve their interests, often at the expense of everyone else.
The Key Distinction: Elitism vs. Recognizing Excellence

This is one of the most important and subtle points about this word.

Not every preference for quality is elitism. A music school audition that selects only the most talented students is not necessarily elitist — it's selecting on merit. An editor who prefers a well-crafted novel over a sloppily written one is not automatically an elitist.

Elitism begins when you cross a specific line: when you start judging the person for their taste, background, or lack of credential — rather than simply evaluating the work or outcome. It also emerges when the criteria used to define "elite" are really about inherited privilege rather than genuine ability. A system that calls itself a meritocracy but in practice only rewards people who went to expensive schools, grew up in wealthy families, or have the "right" social connections — that is elitism dressed up as merit.

The crucial question is: Are people being judged on what they actually do and demonstrate, or on who they were born as and what advantages they started with? Elitism tends to confuse the two, treating the advantages of birth or privilege as if they were proof of genuine superiority.
Why Elitism Is Almost Always Criticized

In modern usage, calling something or someone "elitist" is almost always an accusation — and here's why:

It is unfair. Elitism typically justifies systems where some people have far more access to opportunities, resources, and power than others, not because of what they've earned, but because of who they are or where they were born.

It is exclusionary. Elitist attitudes and systems deliberately shut people out — from institutions, from conversations, from power — based on superficial markers like accent, background, credentials, or wealth.

It is arrogant. It assumes that certain people's views, experiences, and ways of living are inherently less valid or less interesting than those of the so-called elite — which is a failure of empathy and human recognition.

It often perpetuates itself. Elites tend to design institutions that favor people like themselves, making it harder for outsiders to break in, which reinforces the false impression that the elite's dominance is natural or deserved.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Elitism" almost always carries a negative, critical tone. When someone says "that's elitism," they are usually charging the target with snobbery, arrogance, or unfairness. Even people who believe in the value of expertise or excellence will typically avoid calling their own views "elitist," because the word implies an unjust contempt for ordinary people.

You will hear the word used in political debates ("the elitism of the ruling class"), cultural commentary ("the elitism of the art world"), academic settings ("the elitism of Ivy League admissions"), and everyday conversation ("he's so elitist — he refuses to eat at any restaurant that isn't upscale").

Elitism is the belief that a select, superior group deserves more power, respect, and influence than ordinary people — simply by virtue of their wealth, education, class, intellect, or taste. It goes beyond recognizing genuine excellence: it involves looking down on those outside the group, treating their voices and choices as less valuable, and often defending systems that keep privilege concentrated in few hands. It is almost universally seen as unfair, arrogant, and exclusionary, because it substitutes inherited advantage or superficial status for actual human worth.
5089: When you call something or someone elitist, you are saying it reflects — or is shaped by — the belief that certain people are inherently superior to others and therefore deserve more power, privilege, access, or influence. It describes anything that favors an exclusive, select group while looking down on or shutting out everyone else.

At the heart of "elitist" is a specific worldview: that not everyone is equal in worth or deserving of the same opportunities. An elitist attitude holds that a special group — whether defined by wealth, education, family background, intelligence, social class, or taste — is simply better, and that this superiority gives them the right to more.

This isn't just about being part of an elite group. It's about believing that belonging to one entitles you to more — and that ordinary people deserve less, or don't really matter.
Who or What Can Be Described as "Elitist"?

The adjective is flexible — it can describe a person, an attitude, an institution, a policy, a system, or even a culture.

A person is elitist when they look down on others they consider beneath them, dismiss their opinions as unworthy, or treat ordinary people with condescension. They might refuse to engage with people who haven't gone to the "right" schools, or act as though only their kind of people are worth listening to.

An institution (a school, a club, an organization) is elitist when it is designed — formally or in practice — to serve, admit, or benefit only a privileged few, and excludes or sidelines everyone else.

A policy or system is elitist when it is structured in a way that keeps advantages concentrated among the already-privileged, making it harder for others to rise or participate equally.

A culture or environment is elitist when it makes people from ordinary backgrounds feel unwelcome, inadequate, or inferior — not because of anything they did, but because of who they are or where they come from.

• "The new school admission process is elitist — it basically filters out anyone who hasn't had expensive private tutoring."
  • "He can be really elitist about food. He refuses to eat at any restaurant that isn't award-winning and mocks people who enjoy simple meals."
  • "The conference had an elitist atmosphere — if you hadn't graduated from a top university, people barely acknowledged you."
  • "Her elitist attitude makes it impossible to work with her. She dismisses every idea that doesn't come from someone with an impressive title."
  • "Critics called the new arts funding policy elitist because it only gave money to prestigious institutions in wealthy neighbourhoods."
Why Is It Almost Always Used as Criticism?

The word carries a strongly negative connotation in most contexts. Here's why:

Most modern societies are built on the idea — at least in principle — that all people have equal worth and deserve equal opportunity. Elitism directly contradicts this. It says some people are more worthy by birth, background, or status. Calling something or someone "elitist" is essentially accusing them of being unfair, arrogant, and out of touch — of rigging the game in favour of a few while pretending the rules are neutral.

There's also an element of condescension baked into elitism. It's not just that elitists favour certain people — it's that they actively look down on others. That dismissiveness is what makes the label so cutting when applied to a person.

These two words are related but meaningfully different, and confusing them is a common mistake.

"Elite" simply means the best, the top, or the most skilled in a given area. A group of elite athletes, elite scientists, or elite soldiers are just exceptionally good at what they do. The word, on its own, has no moral charge — it's descriptive.

"Elitist", however, carries a value judgment. It introduces the idea of superiority giving someone a right to more — more power, more access, more respect — and often implies the accompanying attitude of looking down on others.

A surgeon can be elite (exceptionally skilled) without being elitist (arrogant and dismissive of others). But a surgeon who dismisses a patient's concerns because the patient isn't educated or important enough is being elitist.

The shift from "elite" to "elitist" is essentially the shift from being excellent to believing excellence makes you better as a person — and entitled to more.
One More Nuance: Descriptive vs. Critical Use

In rare, academic contexts, "elitist" can be used in a purely descriptive way — simply to say that something is associated with or designed for an elite group, without necessarily passing judgment. A researcher might describe a historical policy as "elitist in character" purely to categorise it.

But in everyday speech — which is how you'll encounter it 95% of the time — calling something or someone "elitist" is almost always a criticism. It's pointing out an unjust, arrogant, or exclusionary quality.

If you had to reduce it to its core: elitist describes anything shaped by the belief that certain people are superior and deserve more — and by extension, that everyone else deserves less or doesn't quite count.
